procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (granted decree for possession to Smt. Rattno against Defendants 1 to 3)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated January 3, 1962, of the Punjab High Court in Regular Second Appeal No. 1958 of 1959.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Defendants 1 to 3 appealed to the High Court of Punjab after the first appellate court (Additional District Judge, Patiala) decreed the suit against them. The High Court dismissed the appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Defendants 1 to 3 approached the Supreme Court by special leave after the High Court dismissed their second appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appeal had abated on account of the failure of the appellants to implead the legal representatives of a deceased respondent.

facts: During the appeal, one of the respondents, Ishar Singh, died.
The appellants failed to implead his legal representatives, and their application to do so was dismissed.
The remaining respondents raised a preliminary objection, arguing that this failure caused the entire appeal to abate (i.e., terminate).
A lower appellate court had previously found that Ishar Singh was merely a "proforma defendant" and had passed the decree only against the other defendants (the appellants).
law: An appeal does not abate as a whole due to the death of a respondent if that respondent was an unnecessary or proforma party, and if a decree can be passed in their absence without creating contradictory outcomes.
application: The Supreme Court examined the nature of the dispute and Ishar Singh's role in it.
It noted that the lower court had already identified Ishar Singh as a proforma defendant, meaning he was not essential to the core dispute.
The Court reasoned that the main conflict was between the plaintiff's legal representative (Smt. Rattno) and defendants 1 to 3 (the appellants).
It determined that the relief sought by the appellants could be granted even without Ishar Singh's presence, and doing so would not result in contradictory decrees.
Therefore, the Court concluded that Ishar Singh was an "unnecessary party" to the appeal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the preliminary objection, holding that the appeal did not abate. The failure to implead the legal representatives of Ishar Singh, an unnecessary and proforma defendant, did not affect the appellants' right to pursue their appeal against the essential parties.

issue.issue_text: Whether the finding of fact by the first appellate court that there was no karewa marriage was binding on the High Court and the Supreme Court.

facts: The trial court found that a 'karewa' marriage had occurred.
On appeal, the first appellate court (the Additional District Judge, Patiala) reversed this, recording a finding of fact that the alleged karewa marriage was not proven.
The defendants then appealed to the High Court and subsequently to the Supreme Court, attempting to challenge this finding of fact.
law: The Supreme Court stated the legal principle that the first appellate court is the final court for deciding questions of fact.
application: Applying this principle, the Supreme Court determined that the first appellate court's finding that no karewa marriage occurred was binding on the High Court.
The High Court was correct to accept this finding without re-examining the evidence.
The Supreme Court further stated that it was "no longer open to the appellants to challenge that finding of fact in this Court."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the finding of fact by the first appellate court was binding on both the High Court and itself. Therefore, the court accepted the finding that there was no karewa marriage and did not allow the defendants to re-argue the issue.

issue.issue_text: Whether the property was possessed by the widow as envisaged by Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, so as to make her the full owner.

facts: A Hindu widow inherited property from her husband in 1917, holding it as a limited owner.
In 1954, she was dispossessed of the property by her husband's collaterals (relatives).
She filed a suit to recover possession of the property.
While her suit was pending, the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, came into force.
The widow died in 1958 during the litigation.
law: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, states that any property 'possessed by' a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the Act, shall be held by her as a full owner and not as a limited owner.
The central legal question is the interpretation of the phrase 'possessed by' – specifically, whether it requires actual physical possession or if a legal right to possession is sufficient.
application: The Court interpreted the phrase 'possessed by' in a broad sense, distinguishing it from the narrower term 'in possession of'. It held that 'possessed by' means 'the state of owning or having in one's hand or power'.
The Court reasoned that as long as the female Hindu has a legal right or title to the property and is capable of obtaining actual possession, she 'possesses' it for the purposes of Section 14.

It cited the precedent of *S.S. Munna Lal v. S.S. Rajkumar*, where a widow who only had a right to a share declared in a preliminary partition decree, without being in actual or constructive possession, was still held to have 'possessed' the property.

The Court distinguished the current case from situations where a widow would not be considered in possession. For example, if she had legally alienated the property (as in *Brahmdeo Singh*), she would no longer have a right to it. Similarly, if she were a mere trespasser with no legal title (as in *Eramma v. Veerupana*), the section would not apply.

In this case, although the widow was physically dispossessed by trespassers, her legal title and right to ownership remained intact. Her pending lawsuit to recover the property was an active assertion of this ownership right. Therefore, she was in a 'state of owning' the property when the Act came into force.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the widow 'possessed' the property within the broad meaning of Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act. Her dispossession by trespassers did not extinguish her legal ownership. As a result, her limited estate was converted into a full ownership right when the Act was passed. Upon her death, the property passed to her daughter as a full owner.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appeal had abated on account of the failure of the appellants to implead the legal representatives of a deceased respondent.
appellant_arguments: The failure to implead the legal representatives of the deceased respondent (Ishar Singh) does not cause the appeal to abate because he was a proforma defendant against whom the suit had been dismissed, and the core dispute was between the appellants and the plaintiff's legal representatives.
respondent_arguments: The appeal had abated because the appellants failed to implead the legal representatives of the deceased respondent, Ishar Singh.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the finding of fact by the first appellate court that there was no karewa marriage was binding on the High Court and the Supreme Court.
appellant_arguments: The appellants' plea was that a karewa marriage had taken place, and they appealed the first appellate court's contrary finding, implying they argued it was not a binding finding of fact and should be overturned.
respondent_arguments: The finding that there was no karewa marriage was a finding of fact by the first appellate court and was therefore binding on higher courts in a second appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the property was possessed by the widow as envisaged by Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, so as to make her the full owner.
appellant_arguments: To attract Section 14(1) of the Act, the female Hindu must be in actual possession of the property. Since the widow had been dispossessed and was unable to recover possession before her death, she was not 'possessed' of the property in the manner required to become a full owner.
respondent_arguments: The widow 'possessed' the property within the meaning of Section 14, making her the full owner under the Act, even if she was not in actual physical possession at the time.

statutes.act_name: The Act (Name not specified in text)

cases.principle: Cited with approval for the interpretation of the word 'possessed' in Section 14 of the Act.

cases.case_name: S. S. Munria Lal v. S. S. Ra;kumar
cases.principle: Relied on for its interpretation of the scope of Section 14(1), where it cited with approval the reasoning from Gaddam Venkayamma regarding the meaning of the word 'possessed'.
To clarify that the expression 'possessed by' in Section 14 is not intended for mere possession without title, but requires the Hindu female to have a right of ownership in the property.

cases.case_name: Brahmdeo Singh and Another v. Deomani Missir and Others
cases.principle: To establish that a widow is not 'possessed' of property she has alienated, because the alienation is binding on her for her life interest, and she no longer has any legal right of ownership in it.
For the principle that Section 14 was not intended to benefit alienees who purchased property from a limited owner without legal necessity before the Act came into force.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The expression 'possessed by' in Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is to be interpreted in a broad sense and is not limited to actual or constructive possession, but includes having a right to the property. The section applies to any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of the Act, and does not require that the property must be possessed by her at the specific date the Act came into force.
obiter: A finding of fact by the first appellate court is binding and is not open to challenge in the Supreme Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court determined that the precedents cited by the appellants, which concerned widows who had voluntarily alienated their property, were not applicable to the present case where the widow was dispossessed by a trespasser. This distinction was crucial in interpreting whether the widow was 'possessed' of the property under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act. The court held that a widow who has been dispossessed by a trespasser is in a different legal position than one who has voluntarily parted with her rights.
legal_tests_applied: A preliminary objection regarding the abatement of an appeal fails if the deceased respondent was an unnecessary party against whom the suit had not been decreed.
A finding of fact by the first appellate court is binding on higher courts in a second appeal and cannot be challenged.

The applicability of Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act is determined by distinguishing between cases where a female Hindu voluntarily alienates her rights and cases where she is involuntarily dispossessed by a trespasser.
why_appellant_lost: The court held that the first appellate court's determination that there was no karewa marriage was a finding of fact, which was binding and not open to challenge in the Supreme Court.

The court found the appellants' legal authorities unpersuasive because they all related to situations where a widow had voluntarily alienated her property, which is distinct from the current case where the widow was dispossessed by a trespasser.
why_respondent_won: The appeal did not abate because the deceased respondent, Ishar Singh, was deemed an unnecessary party as the suit had not been decreed against him, making the failure to implead his legal representatives inconsequential.
The finding of fact by the first appellate court that there was no karewa marriage was held to be binding, which supported the respondent's position.

The court implicitly accepted the respondent's broader interpretation of 'possessed' under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act by ruling that the appellant's cited cases on voluntary alienation were irrelevant to a case of dispossession.
